URL: https://www.iranintl.com/en/202611245387
Iran International

Ahmadi, concert organizer Mohsen Lashkari and musicians Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri and Amirali Pirnia each received 74 lashes at the prosecutor’s office in Qom, their lawyer Mostafa Nili said.

Women have been banned from singing solo in public in Iran since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Singer Mehdi Yarrahi, who himself received 74 lashes in March 2025 over a protest song challenging compulsory hijab, shared footage of Ahmadi’s performance on Instagram, expressing solidarity with her and her concert team.

Musician Hana Kamkar also condemned the punishment in an Instagram video, asking Islamic Republic officials what the artists had offered other than humanity, joy and beauty.

Ahmadi’s December 2024 concert was filmed at the historic Deir-e Gachin Caravanserai near Qom, a Shiite holy city and a center of religious conservatism in Iran.

Wearing a long, sleeveless black dress with her hair uncovered, Ahmadi sang alongside male musicians in a performance staged without a live audience. The virtual concert, which defied both mandatory hijab rules and restrictions on women singing publicly, has drawn more than 3.2 million views on YouTube.

Activist Zeinab Zaman highlighted the contrast between the virtual performance and the physical punishment inflicted on the singer.

“Her concert was virtual, but the lash on her body was real,” Zaman wrote on X. “We are recording act after act of courage and shame upon shame in this history. Bodies are eyewitnesses.”

The flogging also reignited accusations of double standards in the Islamic Republic’s treatment of female singers.

In April, as Iran was at war with the United States and Israel, footage of Lebanese singer Julia Boutros was screened at nighttime gatherings of government supporters in Tehran’s Ferdows Garden. Boutros is known for her songs in support of the Lebanese resistance.

Translator Emily Amraee recalled the gatherings in a post on X, noting that the authorities had “enthusiastically” broadcast the Lebanese singer’s performances over several consecutive nights, only to flog an Iranian woman for singing months later.

Others questioned the government’s priorities amid a conflict it has portrayed as a threat to its very existence.

“If possible, in the midst of what you yourselves call an ‘existential’ war, refrain from flogging the daughters of this country. Is that so difficult for you?” Mojtaba Najafi wrote on X.

Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of Norway-based Iran Human Rights, pointed to the government’s failure to address the country’s economic and infrastructure crises while continuing to punish women for defying its restrictions.

“She sang; the Islamic Republic responded with the lash,” he wrote on X.

“A government that is incapable of resolving the crises of livelihoods, water and electricity, yet does not hesitate to flog a woman for her voice, has reached the end of its life.”

The communications office of Iran’s exiled Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi condemned the flogging in a statement on X, describing it as an attempt to humiliate and suppress the artists and accusing the Islamic Republic of fearing women’s voices.

“The virtual concert staged by Parastoo Ahmadi, a young artist, two years ago and livestreamed on social media remains a lasting symbol of the voices of Iranian women who cannot be silenced,” the statement said.

“Before 1979, Iran was a cradle of art and music and women were pioneers in these fields. Today, however, the regime flogs courage and beauty,” it added.

The statement said the Islamic Republic would soon fall and that women would once again play a prominent role in Iran’s artistic, social, economic and political life.

Ahmadi and the four members of her concert team were convicted of offending public decency by producing and publishing what the court deemed vulgar and immoral content online.

An appeals court upheld their sentences in September, including two-year bans on artistic and musical activities and foreign travel.

Amnesty International had previously called on Iranian authorities to halt the flogging sentences, describing flogging as torture and urging an end to compulsory hijab and corporal punishment.
